questions.question: An IT service has met every one of its SLA targets for a full year. From a Continual Service Improvement perspective, what follows?

options.A: Nothing, since CSI is only triggered when a service fails to meet its targets
options.B: The SLA targets should be lowered so the provider can reduce its costs
options.C: The service should be handed from CSI over to Problem Management
options.D: It may still improve, e.g. through automation, lower costs or better experience

questions.note:
CSI starts from the idea that **no service is ever perfect and every service can be improved**. It isn't limited to fixing problems: a service that consistently meets its SLA may still offer opportunities for **automation, cost optimization or a better customer experience** (LO4, slide 3).
Treat CSI as a continuous organizational capability, not reactive troubleshooting.

questions.question: You need executive approval for a CSI initiative that automates password resets. How should you present it?

options.A: Detail the technical architecture and integration design of the new tool
options.B: Show business value: lower support costs and higher employee productivity
options.C: Emphasize that the technology is new and that competitors are adopting it
options.D: Focus on the number of configuration changes the rollout will involve

questions.note:
Every CSI initiative should support organizational objectives, and managers should **communicate improvements in business language rather than technical language**. Executives care most about **cost reductions, productivity improvements, risk mitigation and customer outcomes** (LO4, slide 5).
The lecture's own example links automating password resets to reduced support costs.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly shows the first four steps of the CSI cycle?

options.A: Assess current state → Define the vision → Identify opportunities → Define target state
options.B: Identify opportunities → Assess current state → Define target state → Define the vision
options.C: Define the vision → Assess current state → Define target state → Identify opportunities
options.D: Define the vision → Define target state → Implement improvements → Assess current state

questions.note:
The seven-step CSI cycle: **1. Define the vision → 2. Assess current state → 3. Define target state → 4. Identify improvement opportunities → 5. Implement improvements → 6. Measure results → 7. Sustain momentum**, then begin again (LO4, slide 7).
It starts from desired business outcomes and is iterative, not a one-time project.

questions.question: During a CSI assessment, a service desk records: average resolution time 18 hours, customer satisfaction 72%, SLA compliance 91%. What is the main purpose of capturing these figures?

options.A: To set a baseline that future improvements can be measured against
options.B: To prove to management that the service desk is underperforming
options.C: To calculate the service credits owed to customers for the period
options.D: To replace customer feedback with objective operational data

questions.note:
Step 2, **Assess Current State**, collects performance data, reviews processes and **establishes baselines** for future comparison. These are the lecture's own example figures (LO4, slide 10).
Without a baseline you can't later show that an improvement worked. The lecture also stresses objective data over assumptions at this stage.

questions.question: A team rolled out self-service password reset on time and on budget. Can it now declare the improvement a success?

options.A: Yes, because delivering on time and on budget proves the change worked
options.B: Yes, as long as users have not complained since the tool went live
options.C: Not yet: it must compare results with the baseline and confirm the benefits
options.D: Not yet: success can only be judged by an external auditor after a year

questions.note:
Step 6, **Measure Results**, warns against assuming success just because a project was completed. Compare outcomes with the **baseline** using objective KPIs, **validate the business benefits**, look for unintended consequences and identify remaining gaps (LO4, slide 14).
Success measures should be set **before** implementation begins: if an improvement can't be measured, its value can't be demonstrated (slide 39).

questions.question: A service desk cut its resolution time from 18 to 7 hours, but six months later results have slipped back toward the old level because staff returned to their previous habits. Which CSI step was neglected?

options.A: Define the vision
options.B: Assess current state
options.C: Identify improvement opportunities
options.D: Sustain momentum

questions.note:
Step 7, **Sustain Momentum**, makes gains stick by **standardizing and documenting** the new practice, **training** staff, **continuous monitoring**, recognizing success and starting the next cycle (LO4, slide 15).
The lecture notes that organizations often achieve short-term gains and then **revert** to previous practices.

questions.question: A service desk meets all its response-time targets, yet users keep complaining that technicians communicate poorly. Which CSI data source revealed this improvement opportunity?

options.A: SLA performance data
options.B: Customer feedback data
options.C: Incident data
options.D: Financial and cost data

questions.note:
Operational metrics don't tell the whole story: **a service can meet its technical targets while customers remain dissatisfied**. Customer feedback (surveys, interviews, complaint records, focus groups, Net Promoter Scores) reveals pain points that SLA and incident data miss.
This scenario is the lecture's own example (LO4, slide 20).

questions.question: A recurring problem causes about 120 incidents a year, each costing $200 to handle on average. A permanent fix would cost $15,000 once. What does the financial data suggest?

options.A: Incidents cost about $24,000 a year, so the fix pays back within a year
options.B: Incidents cost about $2,400 a year, so the fix will never pay for itself
options.C: Incidents cost about $15,000 a year, so the fix merely breaks even
options.D: Cost is irrelevant here; only the incident count should decide it

questions.note:
120 incidents × $200 = **$24,000 a year**, so a one-time $15,000 fix pays back in about 7–8 months and saves money every year after.
The lecture's example uses the same logic: 100 incidents × $250 = $25,000 a year, which justifies a $10,000 permanent solution (LO4, slide 21). Financial data makes the case for fixing root causes instead of repeatedly handling symptoms.

questions.question: Which of these is a root cause rather than a symptom?

options.A: Users report that the finance application responds very slowly
options.B: The service desk handles a high volume of password reset requests
options.C: Customers keep complaining about repeated outages of the portal
options.D: The password policy is too complex for users to remember credentials

questions.note:
**Symptoms** are the visible effects (slow performance, outages, high incident volumes, complaints); **root causes** are the underlying reasons. In the lecture's example, frequent password resets are the symptom and an **overly complex password policy** is the root cause (LO4, slide 23).
Treating symptoms gives only temporary relief; removing root causes prevents recurrence.

questions.question: In the lecture's 5 Whys example, a website outage is traced through a server crash, memory hitting 100%, an application memory leak and inadequate monitoring thresholds. What root cause is finally reached?

options.A: The application server crashed under normal load
options.B: A memory leak existed within the application code
options.C: Monitoring standards weren't updated after an upgrade
options.D: The server didn't have enough physical memory installed

questions.note:
The fifth 'why' reveals that monitoring standards hadn't been updated after the system upgrade, so the root cause is **inadequate monitoring governance**, very different from the original symptom (LO4, slide 24).
The memory leak (B) is a contributing cause, but fixing it alone wouldn't stop the next issue from going undetected. The aim isn't exactly five questions; it's an actionable, **evidence-backed** root cause.

questions.question: Customer satisfaction has fallen from 92% to 76% over six months. The team suspects several factors at once: training gaps, slow escalation, frequent outages and weak service ownership. Which technique best organizes these possible causes?

options.A: Fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram
options.B: 5 Whys chain analysis
options.C: Pareto (80/20) analysis
options.D: Predictive trend analytics

questions.note:
A **Fishbone (cause-and-effect) diagram** maps many possible causes under categories such as **People, Process, Technology, Data, Environment and Governance**, and works well in team workshops. Use it when a problem has **multiple contributing factors** rather than one obvious cause (LO4, slides 25 and 41).
The 5 Whys follows a single chain of causes, and Pareto needs frequency data to rank causes.

questions.question: A service desk's annual ticket counts are: VPN issues 260, password resets 190, printer jams 70, email setup 50, other 30 (600 in total). What does Pareto analysis suggest?

options.A: Split the improvement budget evenly across all five categories
options.B: Focus first on VPN issues and password resets, about 75% of the tickets
options.C: Start with 'other', since unexplained tickets carry the most risk
options.D: Fix printer jams first, since they are probably the cheapest to solve

questions.note:
Pareto analysis applies the **80/20 principle**: a small number of causes usually creates most of the problems. Here two categories produce 450 of 600 tickets (75%), so concentrating effort there gives the biggest return on limited resources (LO4, slide 27).
The lecture's own example reaches the same conclusion with password resets and network issues.

questions.question: Using the lecture's impact-versus-effort approach, which improvement initiative should get the highest priority?

options.A: Redesigning the SLA dashboard: medium impact, low effort
options.B: Upgrading the office printers: low impact, medium effort
options.C: Self-service password reset: high impact, medium effort
options.D: Rebranding the IT intranet site: low impact, high effort

questions.note:
The lecture ranks initiatives by **business impact, cost and effort, risk reduction, customer impact and strategic alignment**. In its matrix, high impact with medium effort earns **High** priority, medium impact with low effort earns **Medium**, and low impact earns **Low** (LO4, slides 28 and 38).
Avoid prioritizing on technical interest or stakeholder influence alone.

questions.question: Monitoring shows a server's CPU utilization at 70%, rising by about 6 percentage points every month. If the trend continues, roughly when will it reach full capacity?

options.A: In about 3 months
options.B: In about 5 months
options.C: In about 8 months
options.D: In about 12 months

questions.note:
There are 30 points of headroom (100% − 70%) and growth of about 6 points a month, so 30 ÷ 6 ≈ **5 months**.
This is the kind of forecast **predictive analytics** provides. In the lecture's example (80% utilization rising 5% a month, exhausted in about four months), it lets managers **upgrade proactively** instead of reacting to an outage (LO4, slide 33).

questions.question: An AI recommendation engine reports that password resets make up 42% of service desk workload and recommends self-service reset, estimating $50,000 in yearly savings. What should the IT manager do?

options.A: Evaluate it critically against business goals, risk, budget and governance
options.B: Implement it straight away, since AI recommendations are evidence-based
options.C: Ignore it, since AI should not be involved in improvement decisions
options.D: Let the AI system approve and schedule the rollout to save time

questions.note:
Recommendation engines speed up CSI by suggesting and ranking improvements, and this is the lecture's own example. Managers must still **evaluate AI recommendations critically** against business objectives, risk management requirements, financial constraints and governance expectations.
**AI provides decision support; final accountability remains with human leaders** (LO4, slide 34).

questions.question: Staff in an IT department rarely report recurring problems, because past mistakes led to public blame. Which element of a CSI culture is most clearly missing?

options.A: Recognition of successful improvement initiatives
options.B: Investment in AI-enabled analytics tools
options.C: A detailed prioritization matrix for initiatives
options.D: Psychological safety to raise problems without fear

questions.note:
A CSI culture needs **leadership support, psychological safety, knowledge sharing, recognition and continuous learning**. Employees should feel comfortable **reporting problems without fear of blame**; otherwise improvement opportunities stay hidden (LO4, slide 36).
The lecture names creating this culture as leadership's most important CSI responsibility (slide 54).

questions.question: Continual Service Improvement is described in the lecture as a core practice of which framework?

options.A: PMBOK
options.B: ITIL
options.C: TOGAF
options.D: Zachman

questions.note:
CSI is **a foundational element of ITIL** and modern service management frameworks: the ongoing effort to enhance services, processes, technologies and organizational capabilities to create greater value (LO4, slide 3).
PMBOK is a project management standard (PROJ 614), and TOGAF and Zachman are enterprise architecture frameworks (LO3).

questions.question: A team proposes redesigning an internal tool's interface 'because it would be nice.' According to the lecture, what should be shown before the initiative goes ahead?

options.A: That the team has enough spare time available to complete it
options.B: That the new design follows the latest user interface trends
options.C: That the change can be finished within a single CSI cycle
options.D: Which business objective it supports, and its expected value

questions.note: The lecture is clear: **CSI should never be conducted simply because improvement sounds beneficial**. Every initiative should support one or more organizational objectives and create **measurable business value**, such as automating password resets to reduce support costs or improving uptime to raise employee productivity (LO4, slide 5).

questions.question: Current SLA compliance is 91%. Which target statement best follows the lecture's SMART guidance for defining the target state?

options.A: Raise SLA compliance from 91% to 98% within six months
options.B: Improve SLA compliance as much as possible this year
options.C: Make SLA compliance excellent across all services
options.D: Achieve 100% SLA compliance starting next Monday

questions.note:
Step 3, **Define the Target State**, sets measurable goals, like the lecture's own example of SLA compliance going from **91% → 98%**. Targets should be **Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound** (LO4, slide 11).
B and C aren't measurable or time-bound, and D isn't achievable.

questions.question: SLA performance data shows the service desk's response target is 15 minutes, but actual performance averages 28 minutes. In the CSI cycle, how should this be treated?

options.A: As the vision that defines the desired business outcome
options.B: As the root cause that explains the slow responses
options.C: As a performance gap that reveals an improvement opportunity
options.D: As an acceptable variance that needs no further action

questions.note:
Comparing actual results with targets exposes **performance gaps**, one of the main sources of improvement opportunities in Step 4 (LO4, slide 12). These exact figures are the lecture's SLA performance data example (slide 19).
A gap shows **where** to look, not **why** it happens; finding the cause still takes root cause analysis.

questions.question: A well-designed knowledge base goes live, but staff were never trained or told why it matters, and adoption stalls. What does the lecture say about why improvement initiatives fail?

options.A: Most fail because the chosen solutions are technically ineffective
options.B: Many fail because implementation is poorly managed, not the solution
options.C: Most fail because baselines were measured with the wrong tools
options.D: Many fail because target states are set too far into the future

questions.note: Step 5, **Implement Improvements**, needs planning, resource allocation, **change management** and **communication**. The lecture notes that many improvement initiatives fail **not because solutions are ineffective, but because implementation is poorly managed**; strong leadership and communication are critical success factors (LO4, slide 13).

questions.question: After automating ticket closure, average resolution time drops sharply, but the number of reopened tickets doubles. What does the Measure Results step require?

options.A: Look for unintended consequences alongside the headline metric
options.B: Declare success, since resolution time was the agreed target
options.C: Stop tracking reopened tickets, since they weren't in the plan
options.D: Return straight to step 1 and redefine the organization's vision

questions.note:
Step 6, **Measure Results**, compares outcomes with the baseline, reviews KPIs, validates business benefits and identifies remaining gaps. Organizations should also **identify any unintended consequences that emerged during implementation** (LO4, slide 14).
Closures that come back reopened aren't real improvement, so this change needs revisiting.

questions.question: In the lecture's university help desk example, the share of requests resolved within 30 minutes rose from 50% to 85%, against a target of 90%. What should happen next?

options.A: Abandon the self-service tool, since the 90% target was missed
options.B: Lower the target to 85% so that the cycle counts as a success
options.C: Wait a full year before measuring performance again
options.D: Standardize the gains, then start the next cycle to close the gap

questions.note:
In the lecture's sample answer, performance rises to **85%** against the **90%** target, and the final step is to **standardize the process and begin the next improvement cycle** (LO4, Sample Answer slide).
CSI is iterative: a remaining gap isn't a failure, it's the starting point for the next cycle (slide 7).

questions.question: Monthly network incidents went from 18 to 21, then 37, then 44. Each one was resolved within its SLA. What is the most appropriate CSI response?

options.A: No action, since every incident was resolved within target
options.B: Hire more service desk staff to absorb the rising volume
options.C: Investigate the cause of the rising trend using problem data and RCA
options.D: Lower the priority of network incidents to protect SLA figures

questions.note:
Incident data reveals **recurring problems and reliability trends**, and these are the lecture's own figures (LO4, slide 17). A rising, accelerating trend calls for **root cause analysis**, plus options like enhanced monitoring, capacity planning, automation and staff training (slide 40).
Adding staff (B) only absorbs the symptom; the goal is to remove the cause.

questions.question: A team's 5 Whys analysis ends with 'the vendor is careless', but no data supports it and nothing can be done with the finding. What is the main flaw?

options.A: They needed to ask exactly five more 'why' questions
options.B: The conclusion isn't backed by evidence or actionable
options.C: The 5 Whys can't be used when vendors are involved
options.D: They should have run a Pareto analysis beforehand

questions.note:
The 5 Whys should **validate findings with evidence** rather than assumptions, and its objective is to uncover **actionable** improvement opportunities, not to ask exactly five questions or assign blame (LO4, slide 24).
Blame-style conclusions also undermine the psychological safety a CSI culture needs (slide 36).

questions.question: In a fishbone diagram for 'high incident volume', under which category does 'weak service ownership' belong?

options.A: People
options.B: Process
options.C: Technology
options.D: Governance

questions.note: The lecture's fishbone example for **high incident volume** places **inadequate training** under People, **poor escalation procedures** under Process, **legacy infrastructure** under Technology, **incomplete monitoring** under Data, and **weak service ownership** under **Governance**, the category covering policies, standards and oversight (LO4, slide 25).

questions.question: What is the key shift that AI-enabled CSI brings compared with traditional CSI?

options.A: From preventing issues in advance to correcting them after they occur
options.B: From data-driven decisions to decisions based on experience and intuition
options.C: From correcting problems after failures to preventing them before impact
options.D: From continuous improvement to scheduled annual improvement reviews

questions.note: Traditional CSI was **reactive**: a failure occurs, an incident is reported, an investigation begins and an improvement follows, often after customer dissatisfaction and disruption. Analytics, automation and now **AI** let organizations detect patterns and **address problems before customers experience service impacts**, so modern CSI focuses on **prevention rather than correction** (LO4, slide 30).

questions.question: AI analysis reveals that most critical incidents occur shortly after software updates. What is the best CSI response?

options.A: Investigate the pattern and strengthen testing and change practices
options.B: Stop installing software updates until the pattern disappears
options.C: Ignore it, because correlations aren't useful evidence for CSI
options.D: Add extra service desk staff on the days updates are released

questions.note:
This is one of the lecture's pattern recognition examples. AI turns raw data into **actionable intelligence**, and managers then **investigate the pattern and implement targeted improvements** (LO4, slide 32), here in testing, release and change practices.
Halting updates (B) creates security and support risks, and adding staff (D) only absorbs the symptom.

questions.question: A model predicts that a service will probably breach its response-time commitments next month. Which type of predictive analytics is this?

options.A: Capacity forecasting
options.B: Incident prediction
options.C: Customer satisfaction forecasting
options.D: SLA risk analysis

questions.note:
The lecture's predictive analytics examples: **capacity forecasting** (when resources will become insufficient), **incident prediction** (which systems are likely to fail), **SLA risk analysis** (predicting service-level breaches) and **customer satisfaction forecasting** (spotting declining quality before complaints rise) (LO4, slide 33).
The point of all four is preventive action instead of reactive firefighting.

questions.question: A service desk modernization initiative stalls: funding never arrives, stakeholders resist, and other priorities keep delaying it. What is most clearly missing?

options.A: A more detailed fishbone diagram of the service desk
options.B: Leadership support: funding, barrier removal and a clear vision
options.C: More frequent measurement of the service desk's results
options.D: A larger AI recommendation engine to rank the initiatives

questions.note:
The lecture uses this exact scenario: **without leadership support**, funding may be unavailable, stakeholder resistance grows and competing priorities delay implementation. Leaders **set priorities, allocate resources, remove barriers, promote accountability, communicate the vision** and model continuous improvement (LO4, slide 37).
CSI leadership is a strategic responsibility, not an operational task.

questions.question: A CSI manager funds only quick wins every quarter, so larger improvements never start. What does the lecture recommend?

options.A: A balanced portfolio of quick wins, medium-term and strategic initiatives
options.B: Continuing with quick wins only, since they show results the fastest
options.C: Funding strategic transformation projects only, since they matter most
options.D: Selecting initiatives by whichever team has the most influence

questions.note:
The lecture recommends **balancing short-term and long-term benefits**: a balanced CSI portfolio often includes **quick wins, medium-term improvements and strategic transformation initiatives** (LO4, slide 38).
It also warns against prioritizing by technical interest or **stakeholder influence** (D) instead of business impact, cost, risk, customer impact and strategic alignment.

questions.question: After a CSI initiative, monthly incident volume fell from 500 to 290. What percentage reduction is that?
questions.note:
Reduction = (500 − 290) ÷ 500 = 210 ÷ 500 = **42%**. The 58% option is the share that **remains** (290 ÷ 500). These are the lecture's own before-and-after figures; customer satisfaction also rose from 72% to 91% (LO4, slide 39).
If an improvement can't be measured, its value can't be demonstrated.
